Highlights

  • •
    A phase-field model is developed for He bubbles in Fe under a temperature gradient.
  • •
    He bubbles move up the thermal gradient with velocities faster than in UO2.
  • •
    Stresses in the Fe matrix from He bubble pressure have negligible effect on velocity.
  • •
    Residual stress in Fe can modify He bubble velocities via modified diffusion.

Abstract

A phase-field model is parameterized to study the effect of elastic stresses on the migration of He gas bubbles in Fe under a temperature gradient. Stresses caused by the gas bubble pressure and residual stress in the Fe matrix are considered. The dependence of He bubble migration velocity on the magnitude of the residual stress, average temperature, temperature gradient, and bubble size is measured. In agreement with a theoretical model based on surface diffusion, simulation results demonstrate that He bubbles move towards the high temperature region with velocities in Fe that are orders of magnitude faster than previously reported in UO2. It is found that local stresses in the matrix caused by the He bubble have negligible effect on the bubble migration process; however, residual stresses in the Fe matrix, potentially caused by processing or irradiation, can modestly modify bubble kinetics through pressure dependence of the He diffusion coefficients. Compressive residual stress decreases diffusion coefficients for bulk and surface diffusion mechanisms, thus reducing the migration velocity of the gas bubble. In contrast, tensile residual stress increases the diffusion coefficients, resulting in an increase in the gas bubble migration velocity. This pressure dependence is also consistent with a theoretical model. This phase field model lays the foundation for analysis of bubble coalescence-induced fracture in He bubble-containing steels.

1. Introduction

The high-intensity neutron flux associated with nuclear reactor operation produces displacement cascades in reactor structural components that can generate point vacancies and self-interstitial atoms. This high-intensity neutron flux also produces nuclear reactions, whose products often include transmuted He within the irradiated material [1]. Over years of service, the concentration of He increases, eventually leading to coalescence of atomic He into bubbles, preferentially on grain boundaries (GBs), dislocations and other sites with additional free volume [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. When welding is used to repair reactor structural components that have been previously subjected to neutron irradiation, high temperatures and the strong temperature gradient (e.g. [6], [7] for laser welding) can change the He microstructure, including bubble size and distribution. Unfortunately, evolution of the He bubble microstructure can promote intergranular fracture, thereby threatening the integrity of the structural component [8].
A complete understanding of these processes for He bubbles in common structural materials, such as ferritic/martensitic alloys [9], [10], has not yet been presented. Towards this goal, Yan et al. [11] studied the effects of irradiation temperature on He bubble behavior in Fe-9Cr alloys irradiated by 275 keV He+ ions. They found that the spatial distribution of bubbles, the vast majority of which were less than 10 nm in size, changes from homogenous to heterogeneous due to preferential bubble precipitation on dislocations and grain boundaries at high temperature. The associated transition temperature was around 900 K. Ono et al. [12] studied He bubble formation and migration in Fe and a Fe-9Cr alloy from 200 to 800 °C irradiated by 10 keV He+ ions. They observed bubble migration and coalescence at high temperature and reported diffusion coefficients for bubbles with diameter about 3 nm.
In addition to experimental research, computational methods, such as density functional theory (DFT) calculations, molecular dynamics (MD) and phase-field (PF) simulations, can provide insights into He diffusion and He bubble migration in Fe. DFT has been used to determine values for formation [13], [14] and migration energies [15] of He in Fe. MD has been used to determine the diffusion coefficients of vacancies [16] and He atoms [17]. Unfortunately, MD simulation is not a suitable tool for studying He bubble migration, as simulations are generally limited to a few nanoseconds. Gas bubble migration is dominated by vacancy migration along the internal surface of the bubble [18] and MD simulations have shown that vacancy jumps on the Fe surface are rare events on the nanosecond time scale even at 1000 K [19], [20]. Nevertheless, MD simulation (and even DFT) can be used to characterize the process of diffusion of individual and small clusters of He in Fe. Such information is valuable as it can provide important mechanistic information and input parameters for models at the mesoscale.
At the mesoscale, most PF simulations of void or gas bubble migration under a temperature gradient have focused on UO2 [21], [22], [23], [24], [25], [26], [27]. Zhang et al. [21] found that the modified local temperature gradient around a void or bubble, due to the low thermal conductivity, caused bubble velocity to be more than two times greater than if the local temperature gradient is assumed to be unaffected by the presence of the void or bubble. Chen et al. [23] found that the anisotropy in the interfacial energy can either promote or suppress the deformation of a void into a cashew-like shape. Vance and Millett [27] presented a PF model to simulate pore migration due to the vapor transport mechanism of UO2 molecules through the pore interior under a temperature gradient. Their PF model predicted a change in pore shape during migration from an initially isotropic morphology to either a lenticular morphology or a prolate morphology. Wang et al. [22] found that gas bubble radius has no significant effect on the migration velocity in UO2 when the vapor transport mechanism is considered. The vapor transport mechanism [28], [29] is independent of pore size, and therefore likely dominates for large pores (above several microns) [27].
However, the above research [21], [22], [23], [24], [25], [26], [27] did not consider the influence of the elastic energy or residual stress in the material on the migration of the gas bubble. If the pressure inside a gas bubble differs from the stresses generated due to the surface tension, the gas bubble can induce stresses within the surrounding matrix. In addition, the bubble may move through a region with residual stresses caused by irradiation, welding or other fabrication processes. Compressive residual stress arising from irradiation hardening was reported to be as high as 1.7 GPa in Fe [30]. Welding residual stresses arise as a consequence of the heterogeneous energetic input and can be compressive or tensile in nature [31]. Compressive pressure can slow down the diffusion of vacancies in Fe [32], [33]; it can therefore be expected to have an effect on the migration of He gas bubbles when diffusive processes are the key mechanism. Thus, to develop a complete model for the migration of a gas bubble, the effect of the elastic energy or stress should be considered.
In addition, there are obvious differences in the thermodynamic properties of He gas bubbles in Fe and the thermodynamic properties of He gas bubble in UO2. In particular, the diffusion coefficients of vacancies and He atoms at 1200 K in Fe [16], [17] are approximately 105 times higher than those in UO2 [34] at the same temperature. This suggests that the He gas bubbles should migrate much more rapidly in Fe. Thus, a PF model needs to be developed and validated to quantitatively study He gas bubble migration in Fe.
In this paper, we present a parameterized phase field model for He gas bubbles in Fe and use this model to study He gas bubble migration in the presence of a thermal gradient. This model is intended to describe He bubble kinetics under thermodynamic conditions approximate to welding. Note, the time scale associated with welding is much smaller than the rate of He production during irradiation [35]; thus, the amount of He in the model is considered to be fixed. In the parametrized PF model, two different sources of stress that contribute to the elastic energy of the matrix are considered: stress caused by the pressurization of the gas bubble and residual stresses in the domain surrounding the bubble. Bulk and surface diffusion mechanisms are considered for He gas bubbles in the nanometer size range, coupled to the heat conduction equation. The influences of various temperature gradients, average temperatures, bubble sizes, and residual stresses on He gas bubble migration are measured. Specifically, we find that compressive residual stress can slow down the migration of the gas bubble. However, local stresses around the periphery of the gas bubble due to the bubble pressure are sufficiently small so that they have no significant effect on the migration process. Ultimately, this work lays the foundation for adding additional capabilities into the He gas bubble phase field model, such as coalescence of multiple bubbles, fracture and the interaction between a He bubble and grain boundaries in Fe and Fe alloys.

2. Phase field model and methodology

2.1. KKS model

Several different PF model formulations have been developed over the last few years to simulate microstructural evolution in materials with multiple phases, multiple grains, and multiple chemical components [36], [37], [38], [39]. The Kim, Kim and Suzuki (KKS) model [40] is one of the most widely used PF formulations. In the KKS model [40], the interfacial region is defined as a mixture of the two adjacent phases with different phase compositions but the same chemical potential. With this formulation, the interfacial thickness is decoupled from the interfacial energy, which is a significant strength of this model relative to prior PF models.
In our KKS model, two sets of phase-field variables are used to describe the evolution of He gas bubbles in Fe. One set consists of the concentrations of vacancies and gas atoms, defined as lattice site fractions. There is no need to specify the concentration of the matrix itself since at any point the sum of the concentrations of matrix atoms, vacancies and gas atoms is equal to one. The other set of variables consists of order parameters distinguishing the Fe matrix from the gas bubble. This definition of a gas bubble also embraces the concept of an empty void. Specifically, 𝑐𝑣⁡(𝐫,𝑡) and 𝑐𝑔⁡(𝐫,𝑡) are the concentration of vacancies and concentration of He gas atoms in units of vacancies or atoms per lattice site; r and t are the spatial coordinates and time. The matrix/bubble order parameter is denoted by η and takes on the value of 1 in the gas bubble phase and 0 in the matrix phase. Across the interface between a gas bubble and the matrix, η smoothly varies from 1 to 0. Taking into account the chemical free energy, the gradient energy and the elastic energy, the total free energy in terms of the phase-field variables is written,(1)𝐸=∫𝑉[𝐹⁡(𝑐𝑣,𝑐𝑔,𝜂,𝑇)+𝜅2⁢|∇𝜂|2+𝑓el]𝑑𝑉where the first term is the chemical free energy density, the second term is the gradient energy density, and the third term is the elastic strain energy density. V is the system volume, T is absolute temperature, and 𝜅 is the gradient energy coefficient associated with interfacial energy.
Following the KKS model [40], the chemical free energy density of the system is,(2)𝐹⁡(𝑐𝑣,𝑐𝑔,𝜂,𝑇)=(1−ℎ⁡(𝜂))⁢𝑓m⁡(𝑐𝑚𝑣,𝑐𝑚𝑔,𝑇)+ℎ⁡(𝜂)⁢𝑓b⁡(𝑐𝑏𝑣,𝑐𝑏𝑔,𝑇)+𝑤𝑔⁡(𝜂)Here, ℎ⁡(𝜂)=3⁢𝜂2−2⁢𝜂3 is an interpolation function that describes the volume fraction of the gas bubble phase; its specific form is chosen to be continuous and to have a smooth derivative at ℎ=0 and ℎ=1. 𝑔⁡(𝜂)=𝜂2⁢(1−𝜂)2 is a double-well potential; w controls the height of the energy barrier between the wells. 𝑓m and 𝑓b are free energy densities within the Fe matrix and gas bubble, respectively. The concentration variables 𝑐mv and 𝑐mg are the vacancy and gas atom concentration in the Fe matrix. The concentration variables 𝑐bv and 𝑐bg are the vacancy and gas atom concentration in the gas bubble. In the KKS model, the concentrations satisfy the following chemical equilibrium and mass balance equations,(3a)𝑐v= (1−ℎ(𝜂))𝑐mv+ℎ⁡(𝜂)⁢𝑐bv(3b)𝑐g= (1−ℎ(𝜂))𝑐mg+ℎ⁡(𝜂)⁢𝑐bgand(4a)𝜕𝑓m⁡(𝑐mv,𝑐mg,𝑇)𝜕𝑐mv=𝜕𝑓b⁡(𝑐bv,𝑐bg,𝑇)𝜕𝑐bv(4b)𝜕𝑓m⁡(𝑐mv,𝑐mg,𝑇)𝜕𝑐mg=𝜕𝑓b⁡(𝑐bv,𝑐bg,𝑇)𝜕𝑐bg

2.2. Chemical free energy contribution

In the ideal solution assumption, the difference between the free energy of the solution and its components in isolation is purely determined by the entropy of mixing; the enthalpy of mixing of an ideal solution is zero. Thus, the chemical free energy density of the Fe matrix phase that contains vacancy and gas atom concentrations, assuming that the vacancies, gas atoms, and Fe atoms all fall on a single lattice, can be written as [41], [42],(5)𝑓m⁡(𝑐mv,𝑐mg,𝑇)=1𝑉𝑎⁢Efv⁢𝑐mv+1𝑉𝑎⁢Efg⁢𝑐mg+𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇𝑉𝑎⁢[𝑐mv⁢l⁢n⁢𝑐mv+𝑐mg⁢l⁢n⁢𝑐mg+(1−𝑐mv−𝑐mg)⁢l⁢n⁢(1−𝑐mv−𝑐mg)]Here, Va is the atomic volume of Fe matrix, kB is the Boltzmann constant, and Efv and Efg are the energies associated with the formation of a vacancy and the insertion of a gas atom, respectively. To improve the computational efficiency of the PF model, 𝑓m is approximated by a parabolic function, as discussed in [41], [42], [43],(6)𝑓m⁡(𝑐mv,𝑐mg,𝑇)=12⁢𝑘mv⁢(𝑐mv−𝑐m,eqv)2+12⁢𝑘mg⁢(𝑐mg−𝑐m,eqg)2We take 𝑐m,eqv=exp(−Efv/𝑘B⁢𝑇) and 𝑐m,eqg=exp(−Efg/𝑘B⁢𝑇) which are the equilibrium concentrations of vacancies and gas atoms in the Fe matrix at a given temperature. The curvatures of the parabolas 𝑘mv and 𝑘mg are set by assuming a characteristic vacancy and gas atom composition, 𝑐0v and 𝑐0g, and setting the chemical potential determined from the parabolic approximation equal to the chemical potential of the ideal solution model [41], [42], [43]. The number density, ρ, is related to its atomic fraction, c, as ρ = c/Va. The chemical potential is 𝜇=𝜕𝑓𝜕𝜌=𝜕𝑓𝜕𝑐⁢𝜕𝑐𝜕𝜌=V𝑎⁢𝜕𝑓𝜕𝑐. Thus, Eqs. (5) and (6) have the same first derivatives at a fixed concentration 𝑐0v or 𝑐0g. This leads to expressions for 𝑘mv and 𝑘mg,(7)𝑘mv=1(𝑐0v-𝑐m,eqv)⁢{𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇𝑉𝑎⁢[l⁢n⁢𝑐0v−l⁢n⁢(1−𝑐0v−𝑐0g)]+Efv𝑉𝑎}(8)𝑘mg=1(𝑐0g-𝑐m,eqg)⁢{𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇𝑉𝑎⁢[l⁢n⁢𝑐0g−l⁢n⁢(1−𝑐0v−𝑐0g)]+Efg𝑉𝑎}
In this work, we assume 𝑐0v=𝑐0g = 0.04, which was reported to be the peak He concentration in Fe after irradiation at room temperature using 100 keV He ions [30]. Since choices for 𝑐0v and 𝑐0g are not unique, we tested 𝑐0v=𝑐0g = 0.01 and 0.001. We found no significant effect of the choice of 𝑐0v and 𝑐0g on gas bubble migration velocity results shown in Section 3. From DFT and MD simulations, the formation energy of a vacancy in Fe, Efv, is approximately 2 eV [13], which was found to be temperature independent [33], and the energy associated with a substitutional He atom in Fe, Efg, is approximately 4 eV [44], [45]. Using these values and Eqs. (6) to (8), Fig. 1(a) provides the free energy density of the Fe matrix phase at various temperatures. A comparison between parabolic free energy and an ideal solution model free energy is shown in Fig. 1(b).
In previous work [46], phase-field simulations comparing ideal solution and polynomial free energy models showed that there are no significant differences in the final equilibrium interface locations and order parameter profiles in a single component metal. Moreover, the parabolic approximation for free energy has been widely used in the phase-field simulations of gas bubble evolutions [36], [41], [42], [43]. We extend these previous analyses in Section 3.1 by studying the effect of parabolic versus ideal solution free energy on the migration of He gas bubbles.
The bubble phase is modeled as a mixture of vacancies and gas atoms with no matrix atoms present. The gas in the bubble is treated as a van der Waals gas [42], [43], [47], in which the gas atoms are assumed to have a hard-sphere exclusion volume characterized by parameters b and a. For He, b = 0.039 nm3/atom and a = 0.0034 J m3/mol2 [48]. The chemical free energy density of the gas bubble phase is given by the Helmholtz free energy density of a van der Waals gas [49],(9)𝑓b,vdW=𝑛g⁢𝑘B⁢𝑇⁢⎡⎢ ⎢ ⎢⎣l⁢n⁡⎛⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜⎝1𝑛Q⁢(1𝑛g−𝑏)⎞⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟⎠−1⎤⎥ ⎥ ⎥⎦+𝑓0where ng = cg/Va is the number density of gas atoms. The “quantum concentration” nQ is given by.(10)𝑛Q=(𝑚⁢𝑘B⁢𝑇2⁢𝜋⁢ℏ2)3/2where m = 4 amu is the mass of a He atom and ℏ is the reduced Planck constant. f0 is determined by setting the minima of the matrix and gas bubble phase chemical free energies to be equal (f = 0). Because the minima of the matrix and bubble free energies are the same, the common tangent between the curves is a horizontal line that intersects the curves at their minima (the equilibrium concentrations). Fig. 2(a) shows the Helmholtz free energy of the He gas bubble phase as a function of 𝑐bg at different temperatures.
In a similar manner to the treatment of the matrix phase, a parabolic approximation is fit to the Helmholtz free energy [36], [42],(11)𝑓b⁡(𝑐bv,𝑐bg,𝑇)=12⁢𝑘bv⁢(𝑐bv−𝑐b,eqv)2+12⁢𝑘bg⁢(𝑐bg−𝑐b,eqg)2
The minimum of the parabolic free energy is set to be at the minimum of the van der Waals free energy, thereby identifying 𝑐b,eqg and also implicitly 𝑐b,eqv because the sum of 𝑐bg and 𝑐bv is 1 within He gas bubble (when η = 1). This formulation differs from other PF models for gas bubbles (cf. [25], [26]) that consider the bubble phase to be entirely composed of vacancies (𝑐b,eqv≈0.99) plus gas concentration so that their sum exceeds unity. Note, 𝑐b,eqg changes from 0.245 to 0.256 when the temperature increases from 300 to 900 K. These lattice site fractions correspond to a number density of He atoms in the bubble ng of approximately 22 nm−3, which is in the range of the result of experimental measurements of the number density of He atoms (20 – 80 nm−3) in small bubbles (R = 1 – 5 nm) in a martensitic steel [50].
Because the composition in the gas bubbles will generally not deviate far from the minimum of the free energy, 𝑘bv and 𝑘bg are set by fitting Eq. (11) to Eq. (9) in the range 0.21 < 𝑐bg < 0.28. Fig. 2(b) shows the comparison between the parabolic free energy density and the Helmholtz free energy of the van der Waals gas around the gas atom equilibrium concentration. Fig. 3(a) shows 𝑐b,eqg and f0 as a function of temperature from 300 to 900 K. Using polynomial fitting, we can obtain an equation for the temperature-dependent equilibrium He concentration 𝑐b,eqg = (0.23285 + 4.68 × 10−5T − 2.326 × 10−8T2). Using linear fitting, we find f0 = (-0.236 + 0.00223 T) eV nm−3. Based on the above method to obtain the 𝑘bv and 𝑘bg at different temperatures, a linear relationship between 𝑘bv (or 𝑘bg) and temperature is shown in Fig. 3(b) with 𝑘bv= 𝑘bg = (-21.63 + 0.904 T) eV nm−3.
The pressure inside the bubble can be calculated from the He density using the van der Waals equation of state (EOS),(12)Pb=𝑘B⁢𝑇𝑉m−𝑏−𝑎𝑉2mwhere Vm = (1/ng)NA = (cg/Va)NA is the molar volume, and NA is Avogadro’s constant. From Eq. (12), the pressure inside the bubble increases from 0.45 to 1.78 GPa when the temperature increases from 300 to 900 K.

2.3. Elastic deformation energy

The presence of He atoms in the bubble creates a bubble pressure (Eq. (12)), and the relationship of this pressure to the stresses associated with surface tension can lead to elastic stresses in the surrounding matrix. Moreover, residual stresses may be present in the matrix surrounding the gas bubble, such as those measured in irradiated Fe [30]. These elastic stresses may affect gas bubble velocity under a thermal gradient because stress or pressure can influence vacancy and gas atom diffusion coefficients. Thus, it is necessary to add elastic energy to the PF model to fully characterize He gas bubble evolution in Fe.
Strains are expected to be small so that linear elasticity is used. The equivalent homogeneous inclusion method or eigenstrain method is used to determine the pressure in the matrix arising from the presences of the bubble [51], [52]. In this method, a discontinuous system with a bubble is transformed to an equivalent homogeneous system with distributed eigenstrain. A detailed description of this method can be found in Supplementary Material and references [51], [52]. This method has been used in earlier PF simulations to simulate bubble or void evolution [41], [43], [53], [54]. Alternatively, a stress due to the bubble pressure can be added as an extra stress to the stress computed by the constitutive model. This method is equivalent to the eigenstrain method as shown in Supplementary Material.
Various schemes, such as the Khachaturyan scheme (KHS), the Voigt-Taylor scheme (VTS) [55], and the Steinbach-Apel scheme (SAS), have been used to interpolate stress, strain, elastic coefficients, and elastic energies between different phases in the KKS model [56], [57]. The VTS scheme is used in this work. Even though it has been shown to introduce a larger magnitude of excess elastic free energy than the KHS scheme [58], this excess energy is small compared to the interfacial energies, and supplemental PF simulation results show that there is no significant difference in the stress fields surrounding a He bubble in Fe between the VTS and KHS schemes. Here, the elastic strain energy density is interpolated using the order parameter according to,(13)𝑓el=(1−ℎ(𝜂))𝑓mel+ℎ⁡(𝜂)⁢𝑓bel(14)𝑓mel=12⁢Cmijkl⁢𝜀el,mij⁢𝜀el,mkl=12⁢Cmijkl⁢𝜀tot,mij⁢𝜀tot,mkl(15)𝑓bel=12⁢Cbijkl⁢𝜀el,bij⁢𝜀el,bkl=12⁢Cbijkl(𝜀tot,bij−𝜀∗ij)(𝜀tot,bkl−𝜀∗kl)where Cijkl is the stiffness tensor of the bubble (superscript b) or the matrix (superscript m). 𝜀∗ij is the eigenstrain. The total strain 𝜀totij is written in terms of a homogeneous part,¯𝜀ij, which is an externally applied or residual strain, and a heterogeneous part due to the bubble, 𝛿𝜀ij [56],(16)𝜀totij=¯𝜀ij+𝛿⁢𝜀ij
The homogeneous strain is defined as the average strain; that is, 1V⁢∫𝜀totijdV=¯𝜀ij. Thus, the heterogeneous strain 𝛿⁢𝜀ij satisfies ∫𝑉𝛿⁢𝜀ij𝑑𝑉=0 and is defined in terms of local displacements ui and position coordinates xi as.(17)𝛿⁢𝜀𝑖⁢𝑗=12⁢[𝜕𝑢i(𝐫)𝜕𝑥j+𝜕𝑢j(𝐫)𝜕𝑥i]
Homogeneous strain ¯𝜀ij can be interpreted physically as the strain responsible for the net change in volume of a system, relative to an appropriate reference state [56]. The Fe matrix is chosen as the reference state. For the case of no residual stress, the Fe matrix is forced to have ¯𝜀ij=0 by setting zero-displacement Dirichlet boundary conditions in the direction normal to the boundary along the computational domain boundary. If residual stresses in the Fe matrix are desired, a pressure is prescribed on the boundary in the Fe matrix leading to ¯𝜀ij≠0.
The mechanical equilibrium equation is solved in the quasi-steady approximation,(18)∇∙𝜎ij=∇∙[(1−ℎ(𝜂))𝜎el,mij+ℎ⁡(𝜂)⁢𝜎el,bij]=0where 𝜎el,mij=Cmijkl⁢𝜀el,mij and 𝜎el,bij=Cbijkl⁢𝜀el,bij are othe elastic stresses associated with the Fe matrix and gas bubble.
For a cubic symmetry system, there are three independent coefficients for the stiffness tensor Cijkl: C11, C12, and C44. Based on the experimental results of Fe [59], the temperature dependent elastic constants in the range 300 to 1000 K are C11 = (232.86 + 1.27 × 10−4T − 6.32 × 10−5T2), C44 = (122.82 – 0.024 T + 3.42 × 10−6T2), and Poisson’s ratio = (0.3776 – 5.21 × 10−5T − 8.96 × 10−8T2). At 300 K: C11 = 230 GPa, C12 = 134 GPa, and C44 = 116 GPa. At 900 K: C11 = 180 GPa, C12 = 122 GPa, and C44 = 104 GPa. Thus, stresses generated in the matrix by the pressurized bubble will be temperature dependent. Based on the equivalent homogeneous inclusion method [51], [52], the elastic constants of the gas bubble are assumed the same as the Fe: Cbijkl = 𝐴⁢Cmijkl with A = 1 [41], [60]. A varied between 0.001 and 1 is also tested. The effect of the choice of elastic constants for the He gas bubble on the local stress and the diffusion coefficient of vacancy in the matrix is small. A detailed discussion can be found in Supplementary Material. If the effect of stress due to surface tension, 𝜎st, is considered, the eigenstrain within the gas bubble is defined as,(19)𝜀∗ii=(Pb−𝜎st)/(Cb11+2Cb12)where i = 1, 2, 3. The surface stress is computed considering the interface energy and the gradient of the order parameter [61],(20)𝜎st=[𝑤𝑔(𝜂)+𝜅2⁢|𝛁𝜂|2]⁢𝐈−𝜅𝛁𝜂⊗𝛁𝜂Here I is the identity tensor, and ⊗ denotes the dyadic product. Note, this type of formulation accounts for the geometry of the bubble interface, regardless of bubble shape. Levitas and Samani showed [61] that this approach reduces to 𝜎𝑛=2⁢𝛾/𝑅 where 𝜎𝑛 is the surface stress normal to the surface, 𝛾 is the surface energy and 𝑅 is the mean curvature at the point of interest.

2.4. Temperature and heat conduction

In the matrix, the vacancy/gas atom flux due to a temperature gradient is [47],(21)𝐉i=−𝐷i⁢𝑄𝑘B⁢𝑇2⁢𝑐i𝛁𝑇where ∇T is the temperature gradient and i = v or g. Di is the diffusion coefficient for vacancy/gas in the Fe matrix, which will be discussed in Section 2.5; Q is the heat of transport. The heat of transport of vacancy and gas atoms are assumed equal to the activation energy of Fe self-diffusion (2.6 eV/atom [32]), which is the sum of formation energy (2.0 eV/atom [13]) and migration energy (0.6 eV/atom [16], [62]) for vacancy diffusion. The same assumption was made in [21], [47].
Importantly, the difference between the thermal conductivity of the Fe matrix and the gas bubble can strongly influence the temperature field distribution. Assuming the temperature immediately reaches steady state as the concentration field changes, the temperature field follows the steady-state heat conduction equation,(22)∇∙(𝐾⁡(𝜂)∇𝑇)=0Here the thermal conductivity K(η) is assumed to have the following form,(23)𝐾⁡(𝜂)=(1−ℎ⁡(𝜂))⁢𝐾𝐹𝑒+ℎ⁡(𝜂)⁢𝐾𝐻𝑒
That is, the thermal conductivity in the interfacial zone is linearly interpolated based on the thermal conductivity of the Fe matrix KFe and the gas KHe. KFe has values of 53.6 W/(m-K) and 36.5 W/(m-K) at 600 and 900 K, respectively. The overall temperature dependence is given by KFe = 116.78 – 0.17T ＋ 1.44 × 10−4T2 – 6.02 × 10−8T3 W/(m-K) [63]. Because KFe ≫ KHe, the specific value of KHe and its temperature dependence are not critical, KHe is assumed to take the temperature independent value of 0.152 W/(m-K) [21].

2.5. Phase-field evolution equations

The Allen–Cahn equation [64] is used to describe the evolution of the order parameter,(24)𝜕𝜂𝜕𝑡=−𝐿⁢[𝑤𝑔'⁢(𝜂)−ℎ'⁡(𝜂)⁢(𝑓m−𝑓b)+ℎ'⁡(𝜂)⁢𝜕𝑓m𝜕𝑐mv⁢(𝑐𝑚𝑣−𝑐bv)+ℎ'⁡(𝜂)⁢𝜕𝑓m𝜕𝑐mg⁢(𝑐𝑚g−𝑐bg)−𝜅∇2𝜂+𝜕𝑓el𝜕𝜂]
The parameters κ and w can be obtained from σmb, the interface energy between Fe and He, and the width of the interface lint [40],(25)𝜎mb=√𝜅𝑤3⁢√2(26)𝑙int=𝛼⁢√2⁢√𝜅𝑤where α = 2.94 (for 0.05 < η < 0.95) is dependent on the definition of the interface thickness [40]. The interface energy between Fe and He is taken to be 𝜎mb = 1.6 J m−2 [65]. Cheng et al. [66] showed that surface energies in Fe are not strongly temperature dependent (less than 2% change) within the range of mean temperatures considered in this work. We assume the width of the interface to be lint = 1 nm. Thus,𝜅=3⁢𝜎mb⁢𝑙int/𝛼 = 10.2 eV nm−1, 𝑤=6⁢𝛼⁢𝜎mb/𝑙int = 176.2 eV nm−3. The order parameter mobility L is related to the gradient coefficient κ, interfacial energy 𝜎mb, and matrix/bubble interface mobility Mmb,(27)𝐿=𝑀mb⁢𝜎mb/𝜅=𝑀mb⁢𝛼3⁢𝑙int
Here, for the purpose of determining L, we assume that the matrix/bubble interface mobility is the same as the mobility of a grain boundary in Fe. Mmb is approximately 2 × 10−8 m4/(J-s) at T = 1164 K (80% of melting temperature of γ-Fe, 1455 K) from MD simulations [67]. The temperature dependence of the interface mobility is commonly assumed to follow an Arrhenius relation,(28)𝑀mb=𝑀m0b0⁢e−𝑄mb/𝑘B⁢𝑇
The activation energy for interface mobility is taken to be the value of the migration energy of a vacancy, Qmb = 0.6 eV, because the interface migration is more closely related to the diffusion of preexisting vacancies. From this, we calculate Mm0b0 = 7.9 × 10−6 m4/(J-s). Thus, the temperature dependence L can be obtained using Eqs. (27) and (28). Since the determination of L requires significant assumptions, we test values of L that range between 10−3 to 104 times the value of L determined via Eqs. (27) and (28). There is no significant effect on He gas bubble migration velocity as long as the order parameter mobility is larger than 0.1 times the value of L determined via Eqs. (27) and (28). Thus, the order parameter interface mobility L is large enough so that He bubble migration behavior is dominated by vacancy and gas atom diffusion.
The evolution of the vacancy and gas atom concentrations are described by Cahn–Hilliard equations [68] with the addition of a thermodiffusion term,(29a)𝜕𝑐v𝜕𝑡=∇∙(𝑀v∇𝜕(𝐹+𝑓el)𝜕𝑐v+𝐷v⁢𝑐v⁢𝑄𝑘B⁢𝑇2∇𝑇)(29b)𝜕𝑐g𝜕𝑡=∇∙(𝑀g∇𝜕(𝐹+𝑓el)𝜕𝑐g+𝐷g⁢𝑐g⁢𝑄𝑘B⁢𝑇2∇𝑇)where Mv and Mg are the mobility of vacancies and gas atoms. They are related to the diffusion coefficient Dv and Dg according to the expression 𝑀v=𝐷v/𝜕2𝐹𝜕𝑐2v and 𝑀g=𝐷g/𝜕2𝐹𝜕𝑐2g [46]. The Arrhenius relationship is used to describe the temperature and pressure dependence of the bulk diffusion coefficients,(30a)𝐷v,bulk=𝐷0,𝑣⁢exp⁡(−(𝐸𝑚,𝑣+𝑃𝑉)/𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇)(30b)𝐷g,bulk=𝐷0,𝑔⁢exp⁡(−(𝐸𝑚,g+𝑃𝑉)/𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇)where Em,v and Em,g are migration energies of a single vacancy and a single He gas atom. From MD simulations, D0,v = 7.87 × 10−7 m2 s−1 and Em,v = 0.6 eV [16], [62]; D0,g = 1.55 × 10−8 m2 s−1 and Em,g = 0.039 eV [17]. P = (σxx + σyy)/2 is the hydrostatic pressure in the matrix. V is the parameter related to the activation volume. Based on the relationship between diffusion coefficient of vacancy and pressure at the fixed temperature, V is 0.0037 nm3 for Fe from MD simulations [32], [33]. Surface diffusion and bulk diffusion mechanisms are both considered in the PF model. Thus, the diffusion coefficients are constructed as,(31a)𝐷v=𝐷v,bulk⁢(1−𝑞⁡(𝜂))+𝐷v,sur⁢𝑞⁡(𝜂)(31b)𝐷g=𝐷g,bulk⁢(1−𝑞⁡(𝜂))+𝐷g,sur⁢𝑞⁡(𝜂)Here, the interpolation function is 𝑞⁡(𝜂)=16⁢𝜂2⁢(1−𝜂)2. From MD simulations [19], [20], diffusion coefficients vary strongly with the index of the Fe free surfaces at 700 K; the diffusion coefficients of a single vacancy are approximately 1.3 × 10−10 m2 s−1, 9.4 × 10−9 m2 s−1, and 2.2 × 10−8 m2 s−1 on the Fe (1 0 0), (1 1 0), and (1 1 1) surfaces, respectively [19], [20]. The bulk diffusion coefficient of a single vacancy at 700 K is 3.7 × 10−11 m2 s−1 from Eq. (30a) [16]. Thus, the surface diffusion coefficient is approximately 1 to 3 orders of magnitude larger than the bulk diffusion coefficient at 700 K. In this work, a single surface diffusion coefficient is used in the model and is assumed to be 10 times the bulk diffusion coefficient [16], [19], [20]: Dv,sur = 10Dv,bulk and Dg,sur = 10Dg,bulk.
All parameters in the phase-field simulations retain dimensions with length scale in nm, time scale in μs, and energy scale in eV. For convenience, all parameters used in this model are collected in Table 1.

For all PF simulations, the initial element size is 0.2 nm, which is one-fifth of the interface thickness. The initial time step is taken to be 0.0001 μs. Mesh and time step adaptivity are used to increase computational efficiency, where the element size ranged from 0.2 nm to 0.8 nm and the time step size ranged from 0.0001 μs to 0.005 μs. The concentrations 𝑐bv and 𝑐bg are initialized to their equilibrium values. The initial concentrations 𝑐mv and 𝑐mg are assumed to be 0.001, which is greater than their equilibrium values to approximate the radiation conditions. This initial matrix condition is not sufficient to cause appreciable bubble growth. We also tested initial 𝑐mv and 𝑐mg of 10−4 and 10−5. There is no significant effect of the choice of 𝑐mv and 𝑐mg on gas bubble migration velocity results. As discussed in Section 2.2, experiments showed that He concentration can be as high as 0.04 in irradiated Fe [30]. The evolution equations, heat conduction equation, and stress equilibrium equation are solved using the Multiphysics Object Oriented Simulation Environment (MOOSE) framework [70].

3. Results and discussion

In order to interpret the effects of stress on migration, it is first necessary to analyze He bubble behavior in the absence of any elastic effects. This is the subject of Section 3.1. In Section 3.2, we incorporate elasticity, thereby allowing the effects of stress due to bubble pressure and residual stresses to be clearly identified.

3.1. He gas bubble migration under a temperature gradient without elastic energy

A circular gas bubble is embedded at the position x = 5 nm, y = 10 nm in a two-dimensional (2D) simulation cell x = 40 nm by y = 20 nm. Bubble radii in the range R = 1.2 – 2.5 nm are considered, motivated by experimental observations of He bubbles in Fe and Fe alloys [2], [11], [12]. Temperatures on the left and right ends of the model (Fig. 1(a)) are fixed using Dirichlet boundary conditions. Neumann (no flux) boundary conditions are used for temperature on the upper and lower boundaries. For the phase-field variable 𝜂 and the concentration field variables 𝑐𝑣 and 𝑐𝑔, Neumann no flux boundary conditions are used on each boundary.
The case of Tleft = 898 K, Tright = 902 K, and R = 2.5 nm is used as a representative example to show the key physical behaviors associated with gas bubble migration. At the initial time, the concentrations in the bubble are set to their equilibrium concentrations. Initial concentrations of vacancies and He atoms in the matrix are set to 5 × 10−4. We compare the gas bubble migration results for the parabolic free energy and ideal solution free energy models for the matrix. To improve the convergence behavior, a Taylor-series expansion of the natural logarithm function is used for the ideal solution free energy of the matrix when the concentration is less than 1 × 10−5. This Taylor-series approximation used in the phase-field simulation was discussed in detail in reference [71].
Fig. 4(a) shows the spatial distributions of the order parameter and temperature fields using the parabolic free energy of the matrix after the bubble has migrated for 2.6 μs. The gas bubble maintains a circular shape. The temperature field has a distinct change due to the gas bubble. Fig. 4(b) shows the temperature along a 0.2 nm thick horizontal center line shown in Fig. 4(a). This is compared with the uniform temperature gradient that would be obtained for the case of a constant temperature gradient and not solving for heat conduction. The modified temperature gradient at the bubble is the result of the lower thermal conductivity of the He gas. Similar, although more abrupt, temperature gradients are seen in phase field simulations of thermal conduction across interfaces [21], [24]. Fig. 4(b) also shows that the temperature distribution determined from parabolic free energy and ideal solution free energy of the matrix are essentially identical.
Fig. 4(c) shows the distribution of the concentration of vacancies and gas atoms. For pure Fe under a temperature gradient, higher temperature allows a higher equilibrium concentration of cv or cg separately. However, because gas atoms have a higher diffusion coefficient than vacancies, as shown in Fig. 4(d), a temperature gradient leads to a gas atom concentration gradient in the bubble with low cg on the left (cold side) and high cg on the right (hot side). In addition, because the sum of cv and cg for each site in the bubble is equal to 1, there is a lower vacancy concentration on the right side of the bubble. Fig. 4(c) shows that while overall very similar, there are some small differences for the steady-state concentrations in the bubble between parabolic free energy and ideal solution free energy models for the matrix. On the other hand, Fig. 4(b) and 4(d) show that the temperature distribution and diffusion coefficients are the same for parabolic free energy and ideal solution free energy models.
The bubble and matrix phases evolve to equilibrium concentrations quickly before appreciable migration of the gas bubble. Because there is no vacancy source or He atom source in the matrix in this simulation, the final steady-state concentrations depend only on the initial concentrations. Initial concentrations of vacancies and He atoms in the matrix from 10−6 to 10−3 are tested for both parabolic free energy and ideal solution free energy models. For each free energy model, the bubble size is essentially independent of the different initial concentrations, increasing slightly in area from 19.1 nm2 to 20.5 nm2 for the initial concentrations from 10−6 to 10−3. Thus, the differences of initial concentrations have no significant effect on the location and diffusion properties of the interface. In the following sections, the initial concentrations of vacancies and He atoms in the matrix are both set to 5 × 10−4.
Fig. 5 shows snapshots of the order parameter for two different temperature gradients at 𝑡=0ps and later when the He bubbles have moved across the simulation cell. Clearly, the shape of the gas bubble (in two-dimensional simulations) changes from circular to elliptical for the higher temperature gradient of ∇T = 1 K/nm. This is because of the large difference in the mobility between the leading and trailing edges of the gas bubble due to the high temperature gradient.
Fig. 5 also compares the migration of the bubble using parabolic or ideal solution free energy models for the matrix. It is evident visually that the bubble migrates at the same speed in the two cases. Based on above comparisons and discussions, we conclude that there is no significant difference between parabolic and ideal solution free energies of the matrix for the migration of He gas bubble in Fe under a temperature gradient. As the convergence behavior and computational efficiency of the PF model are both better with the parabolic free energy model for the matrix, from this point forward, we only use this model to study the kinetic characteristics of He gas bubble in Fe.
Fig. 6 shows the bubble displacement as a function of time for various temperature gradients, average temperatures, and gas bubble radii. Note, these thermal gradients are higher than typical thermal gradients induced by welding operations, but not by a significant amount for the smallest gradients studied. For spot laser welding, prior experimental and simulation studies have reported that thermal gradients in the solid region beyond the weld pool are between 0.002 and 0.005 K/nm [6], [7]. High temperature gradients have been found to be necessary in the PF simulations due to the computational cost. Ultimately, we expect that the trends presented in Fig. 6 for the effects of mean temperature and bubble radius on gas bubble velocity will be consistent at lower thermal gradients. Furthermore, we expect the trend presented later in Section 3.2 regarding the influence of residual stresses to also be apparent at smaller thermal gradients.
In every case, the displacement increases linearly with migration time, indicating a constant bubble migration velocity. The velocity clearly increases with increasing temperature gradient, increases with increasing average temperature, and decreases with increasing bubble radius. An analytical model has been developed to predict gas bubble velocity as a function of temperature, bubble radius and temperature gradient [47],(32)vb=2⁢𝐷v,sur⁢𝑄⁢𝑎0𝑘B⁢𝑇2⁢𝑅⁢(d⁢𝑇d⁢𝑥)bwhere Dv,sur is the surface diffusion coefficient of a vacancy, which may be specified with temperature and pressure dependence, Q is the heat of transport, a0 is atomic lattice constant, R is the radius of the gas bubble, and (d⁢𝑇d⁢𝑥)b is the temperature gradient in the bubble, which is assumed as (d⁢𝑇d⁢𝑥)b=32⁢(d⁢𝑇d⁢𝑥) following [47]. Using Eq. (32) and the PF simulation results, Fig. 6(d), 6(e) and 6(f) show the temperature gradient dependence, temperature dependence and bubble size dependence on the velocity of the gas bubble, respectively. Considering average temperature, Eq. (32) has an explicit 1/T2 dependence, which would predict a decrease in velocity with temperature. However, the diffusion constant increases exponentially with temperature, leading to increases seen in Fig. 6(e). The PF and analytical models match fairly well for small bubbles and show some discrepancy at the larger bubble diameters tested, with velocities from the PF model always larger than those from the analytical model. One likely cause for the PF velocities to be larger is the local increase in the temperature gradient around the bubbles due to the low bubble thermal conductivity, that is present in the PF modeling, but not considered in the analytical model. To confirm that differences between the PF model and theory are not caused by the 2D model geometry, Fig. 6(f) also shows one data point for bubble migration using a three-dimensional simulation model with z = 20 nm, matching the y dimension. The difference between velocities predicted by the 2D and 3D simulations is less than 5%.
Our PF model results indicate important differences between He bubble evolution in Fe and He bubble evolution in UO2 from prior PF results [21], [22]. Wang et al. [22] reported a velocity of approximately 4 × 10−6 nm/μs for 25 nm radius He bubbles and a velocity of approximately 8 × 10−8 nm/μs for 2 μm radius He bubbles in UO2. Considering a different bubble migration mechanism and using a different PF model parameterization, Zhang et al. [21] reported a velocity of 4 × 10−4 nm/μs for 10 μm radius He bubbles in UO2. Due to differences in He diffusion coefficients, Fe thermal conductivity and the characteristic size of He bubbles in Fe, He bubbles are predicted to move at velocities that are approximately 103 ∼ 107 times faster in Fe than in UO2. The analysis to this point has not taken into account the effects of stress; we turn to these next.

3.2. The effect of stress on the migration of He gas bubbles

The effects of two distinct origins of stress are considered. First, only the stress in the matrix caused by the presence of a pressurized gas bubble is considered. The residual stress is assumed to be zero. Second, the additional effects of residual stress are considered.
Beginning with the case of bubble-induced eigenstress only, a circular gas bubble is embedded at the position of x = 20 nm, y = 40 nm in a 2D simulation cell x = 80 nm by y = 80 nm. The case of Tleft = 896 K, Tright = 904 K, and R = 2.5 nm is used as a representative example to show the key physical behaviors associated with gas bubble migration. The same boundary conditions for T, 𝜂, 𝑐𝑣 and 𝑐𝑔 as in Section 3.1 are used, whereas two different boundary conditions are considered for stress/displacement: one where all sides are imposed with Dirichlet fixed boundary conditions (fixed BC); the other where stresses on all boundaries are set to zero (pressure BC). In the case of fixed BCs, stresses due to thermal expansion of the matrix resulting from the temperature gradient are expected to be small and thus are not considered.
Fig. 7(a) shows that the choice of boundary conditions and the inclusion of surface stress have no discernable effect on the velocity of a He bubble for this thermal gradient. Fig. 7(b) shows the distribution of hydrostatic stress at 3 μs. Fig. 7(c) shows the hydrostatic stress along a horizontal center line shown in Fig. 7(b). Since the stress in the matrix caused by the gas bubble depends on the difference between the pressure inside the bubble and the surface stress (Eq. (19)), the matrix stress decreases when considering the effect of surface stress. For the different boundary conditions, the difference in the stress in the matrix is small. The maximum stress in the matrix caused by the gas bubble is approximately 0.1 GPa. Stress of this magnitude does not result in obvious changes in the diffusion coefficients of vacancies, as shown in Fig. 7(c). This explains why the velocities of He bubbles in Fe do not change when the effects of the elastic stress caused by the bubble are taken into account.
Next, the effect of residual stress is considered; the residual stress is added to the matrix via the approach explained in Supplementary Material. A range of residual stresses is considered, from 2 GPa compression to 2 GPa tension, based on experimental measurements [30], [31]. A circular gas bubble is embedded at the position of x = 10 nm, y = 40 nm in a 2D simulation cell x = 40 nm by y = 40 nm. The case of Tleft = 898 K, Tright = 902 K, and R = 2.5 nm is used. Fig. 8(a) shows the displacement of a He bubble as a function of time for over this range of compressive and tensile residual stresses. In each case, the displacement increases linearly with migration time, indicating a constant bubble velocity under the applied residual stress state. The migration velocity of He bubbles for different applied residual stress is shown in Fig. 8(b). The migration velocity of the gas bubble decreases with decreasing tensile residual stress and increasing compressive residual stress. Compressive pressures make the exponent in Eqs. (30a) and (30b) more negative, thereby decreasing the diffusion coefficients of bulk and surface diffusion mechanisms, as shown in Fig. 8(c). However, the tensile pressure has the opposite effect, making the exponent less negative, which increases the diffusion coefficients for bulk and surface diffusion mechanisms.
The dashed line and solid line in Fig. 8(b) show the analytical result based on Eq. (32) with the surface diffusion coefficient for vacancies taken as pressure dependent. Two different approaches for the temperature gradient in the bubble are employed. The dashed line represents the assumption (d⁢𝑇d⁢𝑥)b=1.5⁢(d⁢𝑇d⁢𝑥) as is made in [47]. The solid line represents (d⁢𝑇d⁢𝑥)b≈2.5⁢(d⁢𝑇d⁢𝑥), which is measured from PF simulations. When considering the modified temperature gradient from PF simulations, the PF results are consistent with the theoretical results.

4. Conclusions

Repair of nuclear reactor structural components composed of Fe alloys by welding can promote temperature gradients that cause microstructural evolution. To begin to understand the kinetic behavior of He gas bubbles during this process, a phase-field model is parameterized to simulate the migration of He gas bubbles in an Fe matrix under a temperature gradient, including the effect of elastic stresses. The diameter of the He bubble considered in this work is determined from experimental observations and measurements [2], [11], [12]. The phase field model is based on the KKS formulation and the influence of using parabolic free energy or ideal solution free energy formalisms for the matrix is evaluated. The parabolic free energy model for the gas bubble is used with parameterization based on the free energy of a van der Waals gas. The contributions to the elastic energy caused by the He bubble pressure and residual stress in the Fe matrix are measured.
For migration velocity of He gas bubbles in Fe under a temperature gradient, the results of the phase field simulations demonstrate that there is no significant difference between the parabolic and ideal solution free energy models for the matrix. Selecting the parabolic free energy model on the basis of computational efficiency, PF simulations show that the bubble migration velocity increases with increasing tensile residual stress, temperature gradient and average temperature, while it decreases with increasing compressive residual stress and bubble radius. The maximum stress in the matrix caused by the He bubble itself is approximately 0.1 GPa, which is too small to significantly affect the bubble migration process. A quantitative analysis of the influence of the temperature gradient, average temperature, bubble radius, and residual stress on He gas bubble migration velocity is generally consistent with a theoretical model based on surface diffusion in the presence of a thermal gradient.
Importantly, these PF model results indicate important differences between He bubble evolution in Fe and He bubble evolution in UO2. Due to differences in He diffusion coefficients, thermal conductivity and the characteristic size of He bubbles in Fe, He bubbles are predicted to move at velocities that are approximately 103 ∼ 107 times faster in Fe than in UO2. Thus, even for short weld times characteristic of a repair process, the thermal gradient that is generated during welding could cause significant disruption to the He bubble microstructure, potentially leading to bubble coalescence and fracture. Further work will add the presence of grain boundaries to the model and will characterize fracture that may initiate during bubble coalescence.

    Migration velocities of intergranular He gas bubbles under thermal gradients in Fe by phase-field modeling
    Shen Y., …, Spearot D.E.
    Journal of Nuclear Materials • Volume 585 • 2023 • Article 154606
    Citation Excerpt:

    In Section 4.2, we analyze the influence of grain boundary energy on intergranular He bubble migration with bubbles of different sizes and under different thermal gradients. As observed by Wen et al. [32], the local stresses in the matrix caused by the He bubble has negligible effect on the bubble migration behavior. Thus, the influence of local stresses is not considered in this work.

  • Research article
    Irradiation tolerance enhanced by coherent interfaces of FCC/BCC HEA multilayers
    Yang Z., …, Wang Y.
    Surface and Coatings Technology • Volume 457 • 2023 • Article 129338
    Citation Excerpt:

    These results indicate that the bubble migration occurs in the multilayers under applied stress. Although stress-induced He bubble migration is widely observed in materials under deformation or a thermal gradient [39,40], in previous studies on irradiation hardening of materials, the migration of bubbles has rarely been considered, and the irradiation hardening was predicted only by using a simple model in which bubbles are considered as fixed obstacles to dislocation slipping [34,35]. In fact, the effect of the interaction between He bubble migration and interfacial structure on irradiation hardening should be elucidated, because it may determine, to some extent, the strategies to improve radiation tolerance of materials.
